about: Joel's own fixes of passages that passed Pangram but were hard to understand: the examples of what counts in every clarity read's brief (tools/humanization/clarity_read.py). The last three are his rewrites of 2026-10-23 16:55 UTC, each where a reader's plainer version had read as AI; his passed. Add one when he fixes a passage for clarity, with his words.

examples.his_words: "because it was hard to understand due to the compression"
examples.before: The Buddha splits the accounting cleanly in SN 22.22: the five aggregates are the burden; craving is picking it up. The tangle is heavy by nature – even an arahant feels the first dart – and craving keeps us carrying it. Physics agrees that binding is literally heavy: quarks supply less than 1% of a proton's mass; roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy.
examples.after: In SN 22.22 the five aggregates that make up the unified body-mind are the burden (even an arahant feels the first dart) of suffering, and craving is the process that keeps picking that burden up, so that you walk around unaware of the boulder on your back even as you keep making the payments to the Boulder Bank to keep it there (and thank God you can afford to!?). The tangle of the aggregates is what makes them heavy, which sounds counterintuitive since we don't imagine the whole can be more than the sum of its parts in that way. But "binding" is literally heavy in physics too: ...

examples.kind: A shorthand that only makes sense if you already know what he means.
examples.before: The percentage language applies only to partial nibbāna. The fingers and room events were both full (100%) unweavings; body-limited versus body-uncontained describes their scope, not their depth or authenticity.
examples.after: The percentage language applies only to partial unweavings. The fingers and room events were both full (100%) unweavings. The difference between those two was one was limited to the body, one was limited to the room, but neither one had anything that could identify or suffer, and both were the full infinite bliss and release (unlike the 2 birds version which was lacking there).

examples.kind: Terms the reader doesn't know yet ("unification", "relinquish diversity"), and two sutta claims and a conclusion in one breath.
examples.his_words: when a reader's plainer version read as AI ("yours is ai, here's mine that passes")
examples.before: MN 137 tells practitioners to use unification to relinquish diversity, then non-identification to relinquish unity. In MN 121, at every depth of unification the meditator audits the remaining disturbance and finds “just this much – that which depends on oneness.” Unity itself is the last stress.
examples.after: MN 137 gives a two-step recipe. First you use unification (which I'd explain as collecting the mental processes into one attentional direction) to let go of diversity (distraction of the mental processes). Then you use non-identification (not taking anything to be "me") to let go of unity too. In MN 121, at every depth of unification, the meditator checks what disturbance is still left, and tellingly, what they ultimately find is "just this much – that which depends on oneness."

examples.kind: An abstract step with no picture ("Give light a mirror ... reflective consciousness begins establishing a mind").
examples.his_words: when a reader's plainer version read as AI ("yours is ai, this one passes")
examples.before: Physics can’t demonstrate from outside what meditation can disclose within: light sees itself. Give light a mirror through which to see its own beauty, and reflective consciousness begins establishing a mind, which leads us to the Greek myth of Narcissus, who died from starvation due to unceasingly staring at his beautiful reflection in a pond.
examples.after: Physics can't show this from the outside, but meditation can show it from the inside: light sees itself. Suppose light buys a mirror from the local mirror shop, and starts admiring its own beauty. That's like consciousness turning back on itself, and that turning-back is what begins to set up a mind (a "me" doing the watching). Reminds me of the Greek myth of Narcissus, who stared at his own beautiful reflection in a pond so long that he starved to death.

examples.kind: An image the reader was never shown ("no footing") and a jargon compound ("compounded body-world").
examples.his_words: when a reader's plainer version read as AI ("yours was ai, this one passes")
examples.before: Nothing finds footing because no compounded body-world has been established—the same structural reason there is nowhere for suffering to land. Light can be perceived as the material world, but it isn’t an object in the world.
examples.after: Nothing finds footing, because no assembled body-and-world has been set up for anything to stand on, and that's the same reason suffering has nowhere to land (nor anywhere to sprout from). Light can be perceived as the material world, but it isn't one of the objects in that world.
